links.outcome: Content quality and accuracy under low-literacy simplification prompt versus baseline prompt
links.effect: Simplification prompt for low-literacy grandparents lowered C-DISCERN in all 6 models (all p<0.001; Qwen 57.0 to 40.5) with no significant gain in understandability/actionability; medical accuracy stayed Likert 1.0.
links.quote: For all 6 models, text quality scores from Prompt A (Baseline) were significantly higher than those from Prompt B (Simplified) (all p < 0.001).

links.outcome: Understandability of LLM-rewritten patient materials for low-education readers versus originals
links.effect: Rewriting improved C-PEMAT understandability for all 6 models (p<0.01; original median 78.5 to 87.0-100.0), but the simplification prompt did not significantly improve understandability and lowered content quality.
links.quote: The understandability of texts rewritten by all 6 models was significantly better than the original texts ( p < 0.01).

links.outcome: Plain-language comprehensibility of AI-rewritten patient education versus human-authored originals
links.effect: All 6 models' rewritten texts had significantly higher understandability than originals (p<0.01); median rose from 78.5 to 87.0-100.0.
links.quote: The median understandability of original texts was 78.5, while AI-rewritten texts improved to between 87.0 and 100.0.

links.outcome: Medical accuracy and hallucinations in LLM-generated patient education (Likert 1-5)
links.effect: All models had median Likert 1.0 versus 2.0 for human-authored baseline; no significant difference between models (p=0.842) or between rewritten and original texts.
links.quote: Regarding medical accuracy, all AI models demonstrated high clinical safety across the three prompting strategies, consistently achieving a median Likert score of 1.0 [1.0, 1.0] (completely accurate), which outperformed the human-authored baseline (2.0 [1.0, 3.0]).

links.outcome: Consistency of outputs across differently phrased prompts varying in literacy targeting
